The Emulator Box

Eleven real machines, shipped whole — and not one game among them. The Box brings the consoles; you bring the software: cartridges, disk images, and romsets from your own library, loaded from your own files, right here on this machine. Nothing uploads, nothing phones home. Each machine keeps its audit lesson beside it — what was measured, what bends, and what to bring.

11 machines · 11 lessons attached

Finding your way back: from any console, use the browser-style back gesture — Alt + ← or your mouse's back button — to return to this shelf. One honest note: the DOS Console's core asks for cross-origin isolation this window can't give it, so its Play button starts the Baton Box for you and opens the console through the box, in its own window — where DOS runs in full.

The vector machine — jsVecX drawing with light on a dark screen, the way the original's beam did. Mine Storm is built into the console itself, so your first game needs no cartridge at all. It was Steven's first console, ever — a Tempest variation and his first Asteroids.

📦 The Baton Box — the family post office

The Baton Box is a small server that runs on this computer. It serves the DOS Console with the cross-origin isolation headers it needs, and it relays the pass-and-play games — The Relay, the 6502 Bench, the NES, SNES, and DOS consoles — to everyone on your home network: a phone, a tablet, the kids' iPads, anything on the same Wi-Fi as this machine.

Start it here, then open the box in your browser to host or join a game. Stop puts it away. It runs with this computer's Python — the same Python the standalone Baton Box uses — and it only ever serves your home network.
